text: Read both policies as textArrival wins displays 20.00, 25.00, 24.00, 25.00, 26.00. Source versions displays 20.00, 25.00, 24.00, 24.00, 24.00: identical old version 2 is stale, and version 2 with 26.00 conflicts with the recorded 25.00 and is refused. Order 103’s agreed mug price stays 20.00 under both policies.

Read this comparison as textThe customer-only index finds 101, 103 and 105, then dates must be checked in the table and the qualifying rows sorted. The history key starts at customer 1’s newest entry and reads 105, then 103; both qualify and LIMIT stops it. The date-first key reads 106, 105 and 103 to find those same two orders. Order 106 belongs to Edda, so the scan passes it.

Read the three routes as textScanning nested loop: line 1 checks P3, P7 and P9; line 2 checks P3, P7 and P9 again. Six product-row comparisons find two matches. Indexed nested loop: each line looks up its product ID, making two index searches, whose internal page work is omitted. Hash join: read all three products into a hash table, then probe it once for P7 and once for P3. All routes return line 1 with Blue mug and line 2 with Green tea, 50 g.

Read the pruning comparisons as textThe direct October range can exclude September and November, returning E2 and E3 from October. The range from 31 October to 2 November must visit October and November, returning E3 and E4. Endpoint /catalogue supplies no time boundary, so all three partitions remain candidates; E1, E2 and E4 qualify. Applying a UTC date conversion to the key still returns E2 and E3, but the demonstrated PostgreSQL plan cannot use it to prune these time partitions.
